title: Inline functions and variables
recap: In modern C++, inline primarily means that identical definitions may appear in multiple translation units without violating the one-definition rule. It does not force the compiler to replace a call with the function body.

An inline definition must be visible wherever it is used and must be identical in every translation unit. Defining it once in an include-guarded header satisfies those requirements and lets the linker consolidate the definitions.
objectives: Define an inline variable in a header.
Define an inline function in the same header.
Include and use those definitions from two translation units.
Keep every repeated inline definition identical through one header.
warnings: Do not use inline as a demand for call-site expansion; optimization remains the compiler's decision.
Different definitions of the same external inline identifier produce undefined behavior.
A header guard prevents duplicate definitions within one translation unit, while inline permits matching definitions across translation units.
challenge: Create points.h as a tiny header-only component. Define inline constexpr int pointsPerBadge as 4 and inline int badgePoints(int badges) to multiply by it. Include the header from main.cpp and bonus.cpp, then print points for 3 base badges, 2 bonus badges calculated in bonus.cpp, and their total.
hints: Put both full definitions inside the points.h include guard.
Have bonus.cpp expose bonusBadgePoints(), and let main add that result to its own call.
